title: Leave Her Johnny
origin: Traditional pump and capstan shanty sung on the last day of a voyage

pd.detail: Traditional pump and capstan shanty of the British and American merchant service, documented from the mid nineteenth century and in oral circulation well before 1900. No identifiable author.
pd.sourceEdition: Traditional; encoded from the common version preserved in the pre-1930 shanty collections (Whall, 'Ships, Sea Songs and Shanties', 1910; Terry, 'The Shanty Book', 1921-1926)
pd.notes: The words carry their own separate public-domain basis in each section's lyrics.pd; this block covers the music only. Encoded as the traditional common-time version with a swung lilt, not as any twentieth-century revival arrangement or recording. The tune is duple: the call scans as a pickup plus two bars of 4/4, so feel is set to swing rather than forcing a compound meter. The pickup before each call is carried at the END of the preceding section, per the SPEC pickup rule, so no event uses a negative beat.

pd.detail: Anonymous pump and capstan shanty text of the British and American merchant service, with no identifiable author; documented from the mid nineteenth century and in oral circulation well before 1900.
pd.sourceEdition: Terry, 'The Shanty Book' Part II, 1926, No. 27 ('Time for us to leave her'), pp. 52-53, verses 1 and 5

lyrics.notes: Two stanzas, both verbatim from Terry Part II No. 27: verse 1 (the solo line is sung twice against the two chorus answers, as Terry's plate sets it) and verse 5. Whall p. 68 prints the same shanty with 'Leave her, bullies, leave her' and 'O, don't you hear our old man say'; Terry's 'Johnny' reading is the one used here because it is the form the song is known by. The widely sung 'I thought I heard the Old Man say / Tomorrow ye will get your pay' is a revival smoothing of Terry's 'I thought I heard the captain say / To-morrow you shall have your pay', so Terry's wording is kept. The 'wind was foul and the sea ran high' verse is not in Whall or Terry -- it turns up only in mid-twentieth-century revival performances -- and has been dropped. Sung on the last day of a voyage, this shanty was the crew's licensed complaint and carried an unbounded stock of improvised verses; Terry's remaining verses about the beef, the bread and the mate are left out for length, and no offensive verse was carried in from any printing. Each call line begins on a pickup note held at the end of the preceding section, so its bar index here is the downbeat the line lands on.

stanzas.text: Oh times is hard and wages low
Oh times is hard and wages low
'Tis time for us to leave her
I thought I heard the captain say
To-morrow you shall have your pay
'Tis time for us to leave her

pd.detail: Anonymous pump and capstan shanty text of the British and American merchant service, with no identifiable author; the crew answer is the fixed refrain of the song as printed in the pre-1930 collections.
pd.sourceEdition: Terry, 'The Shanty Book' Part II, 1926, No. 27 ('Time for us to leave her'), pp. 52-53, the two chorus answers

lyrics.notes: One stanza: the crew answer is invariant, so both occurrences sing the same words. Both lines are Terry's chorus text verbatim; Whall p. 68 prints the same pair as 'Leave her, bullies, leave her / It's time for us to leave her'. This four-bar section carries the two-line form of the answer, which is what the encoded melody scans; the longer four-line chorus some printings give does not fit these bars and is not forced into them.

stanzas.text: 'Tis time for us to leave her
